The lungs work by breathing air in and out, allowing gas exchange between the lungs and the blood. They are part of the lower respiratory tract, beginning at the trachea and branching into bronchi and bronchioles[2]. The lungs do not expand on their own; they only expand when the volume of the thoracic cavity increases, which happens when the rib cage expands and the diaphragm contracts during inhalation[5]. During exhalation, the muscles relax, and the lungs return to their resting position, containing about 2.5–3.0 litres of air[3]. The inner lining of the blood vessels also secretes angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), which converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, and the lungs help maintain the body's acid–base balance by expelling carbon dioxide[1]. Additionally, the lungs produce surfactant, a surface-active lipoprotein complex that reduces surface tension in the alveoli and prevents alveolar collapse[4].

Helicopters fly by using horizontally spinning rotors to generate lift and thrust, allowing them to take off and land vertically, hover, and move forward, backward, and laterally[5]. When a helicopter is in a hover, the engine provides enough power to counter both its weight and the downward flow of air around the rotor system[1]. As it moves forward, it leaves that vortex and enters a state called translational lift, which provides extra lift[1].

In forward flight, the flight controls behave more like those of a fixed-wing aircraft. Applying forward pressure on the cyclic causes the nose to pitch down, increasing airspeed and causing a loss of altitude. Aft cyclic makes the nose pitch up, slowing the helicopter and causing it to climb[3]. The pedals are generally not needed for forward flight, even when turning, because helicopters do not exhibit adverse yaw[3].

The main rotor or rotor system is the combination of several rotary wings with a control system that generates the aerodynamic lift force supporting the helicopter's weight and the thrust required for movement[4].

The ocean is salty because salt from the weathering and erosion of rocks on land dissolves into the water, and over billions of years, this salt has accumulated in the oceans[3][4]. The main sources of salt are sodium and chloride ions, which come from the weathering of rocks and from volcanic activity[3][4]. The ocean's salinity has been stable for billions of years, as a chemical and tectonic system continuously removes salt from the water[2].

Magnets work because they are dipoles with a north and south pole, producing their own magnetic field and responding to external magnetic fields[1][2]. Each magnet can be thought of as many small volumes of magnetic material that create their own magnetic fields; the force between them depends on their magnetic moments and the fields they experience[1][4]. When a ferromagnetic material is placed in a magnetic field, its internal magnetic dipoles align with the applied field, which expands the domain walls of the magnetic domains and makes the material magnetized[3].

Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator was the Queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt from 51 to 30 BC and the last active Hellenistic pharaoh[1]. She was a descendant of its founder Ptolemy I Soter, a Macedonian Greek general and companion of Alexander the Great[1]. Cleopatra VII was born in early 69 BC to the ruling Ptolemy XII and an uncertain mother, presumably Cleopatra V Tryphaena[2]. Her children included Caesarion, Alexander Helios, Cleopatra Selene II, and Ptolemy Philadelphus[3].

There were other historical figures named Cleopatra. Berenice III, also known as Cleopatra Berenice, ruled between 101 and 80 BC as co-ruling queen of Ptolemaic Egypt[4]. In Greek mythology, the name Cleopatra was given to several women, including one of the fifty Danaids, the daughters of Danaus, and a daughter of King Tros of Troy[5]. There was also a Cleopatra of Jerusalem, the fifth wife of Herod the Great[6]. The name has been used for multiple historical and mythological figures across different cultures and time periods.

Black holes are regions of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape[1][4]. They form when a sufficiently compact mass deforms spacetime according to Einstein's general relativity[1][4]. The first theoretical solution describing a black hole appeared in 1916, and they became widely accepted as a generic prediction of general relativity in the 1960s[1].

A supermassive black hole is the largest type, with masses ranging from hundreds of thousands to billions of times the Sun's mass. Two have been directly imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope: Sagittarius A* at the center of the Milky Way and the black hole at the center of Messier 87[3].

Black holes have been depicted in fiction since the pulp era, and some theoretical objects have been conjectured to match observations via different mechanisms, such as a black star[2][5].

The Industrial Revolution was a major period of change from the 18th to the 19th century, beginning in Great Britain around 1760 and spreading to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840. It marked a transition from an economy based on manual labour to one dominated by industry and the manufacture of machinery, with profound effects on agriculture, manufacturing, mining, and transport[1][2].

The First Industrial Revolution was marked by a transition from hand production methods to machines through the use of steam power and water power. Its effects had consequences on textile manufacturing, which was first to adopt such changes, as well as iron industry, agriculture, and mining–although it also had societal effects with an ever stronger middle class[3]. The Second Industrial Revolution followed the First, occurring in the late 19th century, and brought further advances in manufacturing and industrialization[2][4].

Marie Curie (1867–1934) was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre Curie for their joint research on radioactivity[3]. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win it twice, also receiving a second Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911[3][4]. Her efforts led to the development of nuclear energy and radiotherapy for cancer treatment[4].

Her daughter Ève Curie (1904–2007) was a French and American writer, journalist, and pianist who authored her mother's biography *Madame Curie* and a book of war reportage, *Journey Among Warriors*[1]. Ève did not know her father, who died in 1906 in an accident run over by a horse cart[2]. Marie Curie's work with radioactivity and polonium was her notable contribution to science[5].

Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's lithosphere, which includes the crust and the rigid uppermost portion of the upper mantle, is broken into large moving plates[1][2]. These plates have been drifting since 3–4 billion years ago[1]. The motion of the tectonic plates is determined by remote sensing satellite data sets, calibrated with ground station measurements[1].

The theory describes how the plates move across the plastically deforming, solid upper mantle called the asthenosphere[2]. According to plate tectonics, Earth's lithosphere is broken into sixteen larger and several smaller plates, and new lithosphere is created at diverging boundaries[3]. The plates are composed of two principal types of material: oceanic crust (sima) and continental crust (sial)[4].

Plate tectonics is a subclass of geotectonics and part of the lithosphere, which in turn is part of geomorphology, Earth, and the terrestrial planet[5][6]. The theory explains how the coupling between rigid plates moving on the surface and the convecting mantle drives the movement of the lithosphere[2].
